Fix an integer $d\ge1$. An admitted domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a nonempty bounded Lipschitz domain (its boundary is locally the graph of a Lipschitz function, with $\Omega$ on one side) with fixed $r_0>0$ and $0<\theta<\pi/2$ such that for every $x\in\overline\Omega$ there is an orthogonal map $Q_x$ for which
$$x+Q_x\{z\in\mathbb R^d:0<|z|<r_0,\ z_1>|z|\cos\theta\}\subset\Omega.$$
An orthogonal map is a real linear map with $Q_x^{\mathsf T}Q_x=I$, equivalently one preserving the Euclidean inner product. The map $Q_x$ may depend on $x$; no simultaneous selection of the maps is part of this definition.

A real radial kernel on $\mathbb R^d$ has the form $K(x,y)=\phi(|x-y|)$ for a function $\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$. For a finite ordered list of distinct sites $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, its Gram matrix is $K_X=(K(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^N$. The kernel is **strictly positive definite** if $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every such $X$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$; the nonstrict positive-semidefinite condition replaces $>$ by $\ge$. Only strict positivity is used for the ordinary interpolation solve below.

For an integer $m\ge1$, let $\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$ be the real polynomials of total degree at most $m-1$, with an ordered basis $p_1,\ldots,p_J$, where $J=\dim\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$. The evaluation matrix on $X$ is $P_X=(p_j(x_i))_{i,j}$. The sites are **$m$-unisolvent** for this polynomial space when $P_X$ has linearly independent columns. A kernel is **strictly conditionally positive definite of order $m$** when, for every finite distinct $X$ and this evaluation matrix, $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$ satisfying $P_X^{\mathsf T}c=0$. Thus strict conditional positivity is a strict inequality on the moment-null subspace; it is stronger than the corresponding nonstrict inequality.

For data $y\in\mathbb R^N$, the strictly positive definite interpolation system is $K_Xa=y$. For an order-$m$ strictly conditionally positive definite kernel and $m$-unisolvent sites, the polynomially augmented interpolation system is
$$\begin{bmatrix}K_X&P_X\\P_X^{\mathsf T}&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}y\\0\end{bmatrix}.$$
Whenever the relevant system has a unique solution, its kernel-plus-polynomial function $x\mapsto\sum_i a_iK(x,x_i)+\sum_j b_jp_j(x)$ is called the interpolant. Invertibility for the stated strict hypotheses is supplied by [[lem-rbf-augmented-system-is-invertible]].

For a finite nonempty site set $X\subset\Omega$, the **fill distance** is $h_X=\sup_{x\in\Omega}\min_{x_i\in X}|x-x_i|$. If $N\ge2$, the **separation radius** and **mesh ratio** are $q_X=\tfrac12\min_{i\ne j}|x_i-x_j|$ and $\rho_X=h_X/q_X$, respectively. These are exact geometric quantities, independent of any floating-point solver.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

A matrix $A\in M_n(F)$ is **invertible** when there is a matrix $B\in M_n(F)$
such that

$$AB=I_n=BA.$$

Such a $B$ is unique and is denoted $A^{-1}$. The **general linear set** is

$$\operatorname{GL}_n(F):=\{A\in M_n(F):A\text{ is invertible}\}.$$

It is the set of units of the ring $M_n(F)$. The fact that it is a group under
matrix multiplication is [[cor-general-linear-group-is-a-group]]. For $n=0$,
the unique empty matrix is $I_0$ and is its own inverse.

derivations.claim: In the strictly positive definite case, if $K_Xa=0$, then $a^{\mathsf T}K_Xa=0$, so [F1] forces $a=0$. Thus the linear map $a\mapsto K_Xa$ has zero kernel.

In the augmented case, let $\begin{bmatrix}K_X&P_X\\P_X^{\mathsf T}&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\end{bmatrix}=0$. The lower block gives $P_X^{\mathsf T}a=0$, and multiplying the upper block by $a^{\mathsf T}$ gives $a^{\mathsf T}K_Xa+a^{\mathsf T}P_Xb=0$. Since $a^{\mathsf T}P_X=(P_X^{\mathsf T}a)^{\mathsf T}=0$, strict conditional positivity [F2] forces $a=0$.
By [F3], its rank is $N$, so it is onto $\mathbb R^N$ as well as one-to-one; [F5] makes $K_X$ invertible and each system $K_Xa=y$ has a unique solution.

With $a=0$, the upper block reduces to $P_Xb=0$. The columns of $P_X$ are linearly independent by [F2], so $b=0$. The augmented matrix is square; [F3] now gives full rank and surjectivity, and [F5] gives a unique solution for every right-hand side.

Assume the Axiom of Choice when using the well-definedness results below; it is inherited conservatively from the published $L^2$ completeness supplier. Let $d\ge1$ and $s>d/2$. Write $L^2_s(\mathbb R^d)$ for the equivalence classes modulo Lebesgue-almost-everywhere equality of measurable complex functions $g$ satisfying
$$\|g\|_{L^2_s}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^d}(1+|\xi|^2)^s|g(\xi)|^2\,d\xi<\infty.$$
For such $g$, the **inverse Fourier representative** is the function
$$U_g(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}g(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The whole-space Bessel-potential space $H^s(\mathbb R^d)$ consists of these representatives, with norm $\|U_g\|_{H^s(\mathbb R^d)}=\|g\|_{L^2_s}$. For the admitted domain $\Omega$ of [[def-rbf-kernels-sites-and-augmented-interpolation]], define $H^s(\Omega)$ to be the restrictions $U|_\Omega$ of whole-space members, with the quotient norm
$$\|u\|_{H^s(\Omega)}=\inf\{\|U\|_{H^s(\mathbb R^d)}:U|_\Omega=u\}.$$
The whole-space inner product is $\langle U_g,U_h\rangle_{H^s}=\int (1+|\xi|^2)^s g(\xi)\overline{h(\xi)}\,d\xi$, linear in the first variable as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].
The inverse Fourier map is injective, whole-space representatives are continuous, the whole-space model is Hilbert, and Schwartz functions are dense in that norm; these facts are supplied by [[lem-matern-weighted-fourier-space-is-hilbert-and-injective]] and [[lem-schwartz-dense-in-fourier-bessel-potential-space]]. The restriction quotient is a norm by bounded point evaluation; its Hilbert realization as the restricted native space is proved in [[lem-restricted-matern-native-space-is-sobolev]]. No extension operator or identification with an intrinsic fractional Sobolev norm on $\Omega$ is part of this definition.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,

Let $f$ be any Schwartz function and define $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$. Integration by parts on finite boxes, with boundary terms tending to zero by [F5], shows that every $\xi^\gamma D_\xi^\alpha\widehat f(\xi)$ is a finite linear combination of Fourier transforms of derivatives of polynomial multiples of $f$. Each such function is in $L^1$ by [F5], so its Fourier transform is bounded; hence $\widehat f$ is Schwartz and in $L^1$. In particular $\int(1+|\xi|^2)^s|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi<\infty$, by polar integration [F6].

On the bounded ball $O=B(0,R+1)$, the weight $(1+|\xi|^2)^s$ is bounded above by a finite constant $C_R$. The restriction of $g_R$ to $O$ lies in $L^2(O)$, so [F2] gives $\phi\in C_c^\infty(O)$ with $\|g_R-\phi\|_{L^2(O)}<\varepsilon/(2\sqrt{C_R})$. Extending $\phi$ by zero is still smooth and compactly supported on $\mathbb R^d$ because its support is compactly contained in $O$, and $$\|g_R-\phi\|_{L^2_s}^2\le C_R\|g_R-\phi\|_{L^2(O)}^2<\varepsilon^2/4.$$

For $\epsilon>0$, absolute Fubini [F6] and the Gaussian transform [F6] give $$\int\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}e^{-\pi\epsilon|\xi|^2}d\xi=\int f(y)\epsilon^{-d/2}e^{-\pi|x-y|^2/\epsilon}dy=(f*G_\epsilon)(x),$$ where $G_\epsilon(z)=\epsilon^{-d/2}e^{-\pi|z|^2/\epsilon}$. $$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Since $w=A(a^2+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{-s}$, the two positive functions $(a^2+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^s$ and $(1+|\xi|^2)^s$ have ratio bounded above and below by positive constants: compare $a^2+4\pi^2r^2$ with $1+r^2$ separately using the minimum and maximum of $a^2$ and $4\pi^2$. Multiplying by $A^{-1}$ and taking square roots gives the displayed norm equivalence. Thus the weighted $L^2$ norms defining $\mathcal H_k$ and $H^s$ are equivalent and have the same representatives by injectivity [F1,F2]; completeness of $H^s$ implies completeness of $\mathcal H_k$.

For a complex coefficient vector $c=(c_j)$, the Hermitian quadratic form of the Gram matrix is $$c^*K_Xc=\int_{\mathbb R^d}w(\xi)\left|\sum_{j=1}^Nc_je^{-2\pi ix_j\cdot\xi}\right|^2d\xi.$$ If it is zero, positivity of $w$ implies the continuous exponential sum is zero almost everywhere. A continuous function zero almost everywhere is zero everywhere, because any point of nonzero value would have a neighborhood on which its modulus is bounded below, and such a neighborhood contains a positive-measure box [F5].

The spectral representative of $k(\cdot-y)$ is $w(\xi)e^{-2\pi i y\cdot\xi}$. Its $\mathcal H_k$ norm squared is $\int w=1$, and for $U_g\in\mathcal H_k$, $$\langle U_g,k(\cdot-y)\rangle_k=\int g(\xi)e^{2\pi i y\cdot\xi}d\xi=U_g(y).$$ The integral exists because Cauchy--Schwarz bounds $\int|g|$ by $\|g\|_k(\int w)^{1/2}$. Hence point evaluation is continuous and the stated kernel sections reproduce it.

If $U$ is orthogonal to every section centered at $y\in\mathbb R^d$, step 2.1 gives $U(y)=0$ for every $y$. Fourier injectivity [F1] then makes $U=0$ in $\mathcal H_k$. By [F3] the span of all sections is dense.

Choose $v=(1,t,\ldots,t^{d-1})$ so that the numbers $v\cdot x_j$ are pairwise distinct. For each pair $i
e j$, the polynomial $(x_i-x_j)\cdot(1,t,\ldots,t^{d-1})$ is nonzero because $x_i-x_j
e0$; [F4] says its zero set is finite. The ordered field $\mathbb R$ has $0<1$, so the natural multiples $0,1,1+1,\ldots$ are strictly increasing and $\mathbb R$ is infinite. Thus a real $t$ exists outside the finite union of root sets. Restrict the vanishing exponential sum to $\xi=uv$ and differentiate at $u=0$ for orders $r=0,\ldots,N-1$. This gives $\sum_jc_j(v\cdot x_j)^r=0$. For each $j$, the Lagrange polynomial $$L_j(t)=\prod_{i
e j} rac{t-v\cdot x_i}{v\cdot x_j-v\cdot x_i}$$ has degree at most $N-1$ and satisfies $L_j(v\cdot x_i)=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise. Taking the same linear combination of the moment equations as the coefficients of $L_j$ yields $c_j=0$. Thus all $c_j=0$, and the real Gram matrix is strictly positive definite.

derivations.claim: The set $\mathcal N_\Omega$ is a linear subspace. If $U_n\in\mathcal N_\Omega$ converges to $U$ in native norm, then for each $x\in\Omega$, [F2] gives $|U_n(x)-U(x)|\le C_x\|U_n-U\|_k\to0$; hence $U(x)=0$ and $U\in\mathcal N_\Omega$. Thus $\mathcal N_\Omega$ is closed.

By [F3], each equivalence class modulo $\mathcal N_\Omega$ has a unique representative in $\mathcal N_\Omega^\perp$, namely its orthogonal projection onto that complement; its norm is the infimum of the norms of all extensions because adding an element of $\mathcal N_\Omega$ changes only the nullspace component. Therefore the restriction quotient is a Hilbert space isometric to $\mathcal N_\Omega^\perp$.

For $y\in\Omega$, the section $k_y=k(\cdot-y)$ lies in $\mathcal N_\Omega^\perp$: for every $N\in\mathcal N_\Omega$, $\langle N,k_y\rangle_k=N(y)=0$ by reproduction [F2]. Its induced quotient element therefore represents the restricted kernel section, and it reproduces evaluation of each restricted function at $y$.

If $U\in\mathcal N_\Omega^\perp$ is orthogonal to every $k_y$ with $y\in\Omega$, then [F2] gives $U(y)=0$ for all $y\in\Omega$, so $U\in\mathcal N_\Omega$. Thus $U\in\mathcal N_\Omega\cap\mathcal N_\Omega^\perp=\{0\}$. The restricted kernel sections span densely in $\mathcal N_\Omega^\perp$, which proves that the quotient is exactly the RKHS of the restricted kernel.

Every extension $U$ of $u$ satisfies $c_0\|U\|_{H^s(\mathbb R^d)}\le\|U\|_k\le C_0\|U\|_{H^s(\mathbb R^d)}$ by [F1]. Taking the infimum over the same set of extensions on both sides gives $c_0\|u\|_{H^s(\Omega)}\le\|u\|_{\mathcal H_k(\Omega)}\le C_0\|u\|_{H^s(\Omega)}$.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. An admitted domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a nonempty bounded Lipschitz domain (its boundary is locally the graph of a Lipschitz function, with $\Omega$ on one side) with fixed $r_0>0$ and $0<\theta<\pi/2$ such that for every $x\in\overline\Omega$ there is an orthogonal map $Q_x$ for which
$$x+Q_x\{z\in\mathbb R^d:0<|z|<r_0,\ z_1>|z|\cos\theta\}\subset\Omega.$$
An orthogonal map is a real linear map with $Q_x^{\mathsf T}Q_x=I$, equivalently one preserving the Euclidean inner product. The map $Q_x$ may depend on $x$; no simultaneous selection of the maps is part of this definition.

A real radial kernel on $\mathbb R^d$ has the form $K(x,y)=\phi(|x-y|)$ for a function $\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$. For a finite ordered list of distinct sites $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, its Gram matrix is $K_X=(K(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^N$. The kernel is **strictly positive definite** if $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every such $X$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$; the nonstrict positive-semidefinite condition replaces $>$ by $\ge$. Only strict positivity is used for the ordinary interpolation solve below.

For an integer $m\ge1$, let $\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$ be the real polynomials of total degree at most $m-1$, with an ordered basis $p_1,\ldots,p_J$, where $J=\dim\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$. The evaluation matrix on $X$ is $P_X=(p_j(x_i))_{i,j}$. The sites are **$m$-unisolvent** for this polynomial space when $P_X$ has linearly independent columns. A kernel is **strictly conditionally positive definite of order $m$** when, for every finite distinct $X$ and this evaluation matrix, $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$ satisfying $P_X^{\mathsf T}c=0$. Thus strict conditional positivity is a strict inequality on the moment-null subspace; it is stronger than the corresponding nonstrict inequality.

For data $y\in\mathbb R^N$, the strictly positive definite interpolation system is $K_Xa=y$. For an order-$m$ strictly conditionally positive definite kernel and $m$-unisolvent sites, the polynomially augmented interpolation system is
$$\begin{bmatrix}K_X&P_X\\P_X^{\mathsf T}&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}y\\0\end{bmatrix}.$$
Whenever the relevant system has a unique solution, its kernel-plus-polynomial function $x\mapsto\sum_i a_iK(x,x_i)+\sum_j b_jp_j(x)$ is called the interpolant. Invertibility for the stated strict hypotheses is supplied by [[lem-rbf-augmented-system-is-invertible]].

For a finite nonempty site set $X\subset\Omega$, the **fill distance** is $h_X=\sup_{x\in\Omega}\min_{x_i\in X}|x-x_i|$. If $N\ge2$, the **separation radius** and **mesh ratio** are $q_X=\tfrac12\min_{i\ne j}|x_i-x_j|$ and $\rho_X=h_X/q_X$, respectively. These are exact geometric quantities, independent of any floating-point solver.

derivations.claim: The evaluations at points of the open unit cone $C=\{z:0<|z|<1,\ z_1>|z|\cos\theta\}$ span the dual of $\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$. $\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the

formulas above are not asserted in this case.

([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the

Let $(w,v)$ be the exact output of that procedure and put $r_Y=\max_i|y_i-x|$. Then the procedure returns success, and for every $q\in\Pi_p$,
$$\sum_{i=1}^Nw_iq(y_i)=Lq(x).$$
If $f\in C^{p+1}(U)$ on an open convex set $U$ containing the compact convex hull $H=\operatorname{conv}\{x,y_1,\ldots,y_N\}$, then

Consequently, a separately proved bound $\sum_i|w_i|\le C_wr_Y^{-t}$ yields the order $C_{d,p}C_wr_Y^{p+1-t}$ truncation bound. Unisolvence alone is not asserted to provide this weight-norm bound.

Here $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d$, $|\alpha|=\sum_j\alpha_j$, and $D^\alpha$ is the corresponding partial derivative. All arithmetic in this procedure is exact real arithmetic.

If dimensions, distinctness, unisolvence, the kernel condition, or derivative availability fail, return `inadmissible-input`. Otherwise form $P_{ij}=p_j(y_i)$, $b_i=(L_zK(z,y_i))|_{z=x}$, $\ell_j=(Lp_j)(x)$, and
$$M=\begin{bmatrix}K_Y&P\\P^{\mathsf T}&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad g=\begin{bmatrix}b\\ell\end{bmatrix}.$$
Solve $Mz=g$ by exact Gaussian elimination with deterministic partial row pivoting: set $A=M$, $c=g$, and $n=N+J$. For $k=1,\ldots,n$, choose the least $i\ge k$ with $A_{ik}\ne0$; if none exists, return `singular-system`. Swap rows $i$ and $k$ in both $A$ and $c$. For each $j=k+1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order, set $\mu=A_{jk}/A_{kk}$, replace row $j$ by row $j-\mu\,\mathrm{row}_k$ in $A$ and $c$, and set $A_{jk}=0$. After all pivots, solve the resulting upper-triangular system by descending substitution. Return `success` with the first $N$ coordinates $w$ of $z$ and the remaining $J$ polynomial multipliers. The stated strict hypotheses imply that `singular-system` is unreachable, as proved by [[lem-rbf-augmented-system-is-invertible]].

The returned $w$ is an exact mathematical weight vector. The nonsingularity lemma [[lem-rbf-augmented-system-is-invertible]] makes `singular-system` unreachable for every input that passes the stated strict hypotheses. This definition makes no floating-point stability or solver-error claim.

Let $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$ be a finite ordered list of distinct sites in $\mathbb R^d$. If $K$ is strictly positive definite, then $K_X$ is invertible and $K_Xa=y$ has a unique solution for every $y\in\mathbb R^N$. Fix an integer $d\ge1$. $$x+Q_x\{z\in\mathbb R^d:0<|z|<r_0,\ z_1>|z|\cos\theta\}\subset\Omega.$$
An orthogonal map is a real linear map with $Q_x^{\mathsf T}Q_x=I$, equivalently one preserving the Euclidean inner product. The map $Q_x$ may depend on $x$; no simultaneous selection of the maps is part of this definition.

A real radial kernel on $\mathbb R^d$ has the form $K(x,y)=\phi(|x-y|)$ for a function $\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$. For a finite ordered list of distinct sites $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, its Gram matrix is $K_X=(K(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^N$. Only strict positivity is used for the ordinary interpolation solve below.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. An admitted domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a nonempty bounded Lipschitz domain (its boundary is locally the graph of a Lipschitz function, with $\Omega$ on one side) with fixed $r_0>0$ and $0<\theta<\pi/2$ such that for every $x\in\overline\Omega$ there is an orthogonal map $Q_x$ for which
$$x+Q_x\{z\in\mathbb R^d:0<|z|<r_0,\ z_1>|z|\cos\theta\}\subset\Omega.$$
An orthogonal map is a real linear map with $Q_x^{\mathsf T}Q_x=I$, equivalently one preserving the Euclidean inner product. The map $Q_x$ may depend on $x$; no simultaneous selection of the maps is part of this definition.

A real radial kernel on $\mathbb R^d$ has the form $K(x,y)=\phi(|x-y|)$ for a function $\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$. For a finite ordered list of distinct sites $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, its Gram matrix is $K_X=(K(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^N$. The kernel is **strictly positive definite** if $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every such $X$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$; the nonstrict positive-semidefinite condition replaces $>$ by $\ge$. Only strict positivity is used for the ordinary interpolation solve below.

For an integer $m\ge1$, let $\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$ be the real polynomials of total degree at most $m-1$, with an ordered basis $p_1,\ldots,p_J$, where $J=\dim\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$. The evaluation matrix on $X$ is $P_X=(p_j(x_i))_{i,j}$. The sites are **$m$-unisolvent** for this polynomial space when $P_X$ has linearly independent columns. A kernel is **strictly conditionally positive definite of order $m$** when, for every finite distinct $X$ and this evaluation matrix, $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$ satisfying $P_X^{\mathsf T}c=0$. Thus strict conditional positivity is a strict inequality on the moment-null subspace; it is stronger than the corresponding nonstrict inequality.

For data $y\in\mathbb R^N$, the strictly positive definite interpolation system is $K_Xa=y$. For an order-$m$ strictly conditionally positive definite kernel and $m$-unisolvent sites, the polynomially augmented interpolation system is
$$\begin{bmatrix}K_X&P_X\\P_X^{\mathsf T}&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}y\\0\end{bmatrix}.$$
Whenever the relevant system has a unique solution, its kernel-plus-polynomial function $x\mapsto\sum_i a_iK(x,x_i)+\sum_j b_jp_j(x)$ is called the interpolant. Invertibility for the stated strict hypotheses is supplied by [[lem-rbf-augmented-system-is-invertible]].

For a finite nonempty site set $X\subset\Omega$, the **fill distance** is $h_X=\sup_{x\in\Omega}\min_{x_i\in X}|x-x_i|$. If $N\ge2$, the **separation radius** and **mesh ratio** are $q_X=\tfrac12\min_{i\ne j}|x_i-x_j|$ and $\rho_X=h_X/q_X$, respectively. These are exact geometric quantities, independent of any floating-point solver.

If $T$ is self-adjoint on a nonzero finite-dimensional real inner product space and its
eigenvalues are ordered as

$$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n,$$

then

$$\lambda_1=\max_{v\ne0} R_T(v)\qquad\text{and}\qquad \lambda_n=\min_{v\ne0} R_T(v).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $n\ge 1$, let either $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with
$p\ge 1$ or $p=\infty$, and let
$A\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ be an invertible real matrix
([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]), so that the linear system
$Ax=b$ has the unique solution $x=A^{-1}b$ for every right-hand side
$b\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$. The **condition number of the linear system** (equivalently,
of the matrix $A$) with respect to the induced $p$-norm of
[[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]], using its separately defined infinity case when
$p=\infty$, is

$$\kappa_p(A)\;:=\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert A^{-1}\rVert_p\;\in\;[1,+\infty).$$

**The value is at least one and is never infinite.** The inverse $A^{-1}$ is the
unique two-sided inverse of $A$ ([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]),
so $AA^{-1}=I_n$ and $A^{-1}A=I_n$. For rational finite $p$,
submultiplicativity and normalisation are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]].
For $p=\infty$, the same properties follow directly from the defining
supremum: $\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\lVert A\rVert_\infty\lVert x\rVert_\infty$
and applying this estimate twice gives submultiplicativity, while
$I_nx=x$ gives $\lVert I_n\rVert_\infty=1$. Hence in either case

$$1=\lVert I_n\rVert_p=\lVert AA^{-1}\rVert_p\le\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert A^{-1}\rVert_p=\kappa_p(A).$$

Equivalently, $\kappa_p(A)$ is the product of the largest factor by which $A$
stretches a nonzero vector and the largest factor by which $A^{-1}$ stretches
one. Applying the same estimate to $A^{-1}$ in place of $A$ gives
$\kappa_p(A^{-1})=\kappa_p(A)$.

derivations.claim: The cube satisfies the uniform cone condition. For $x\in[0,1]^d$, choose signs $\sigma_j=1$ if $x_j\le1/2$ and $-1$ otherwise, and put $u=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_d)/\sqrt d$. If $u=e_1$ take $Q_x=I$; otherwise put $v=(e_1-u)/|e_1-u|$ and $Q_x=I-2vv^{\mathsf T}$, which is orthogonal and sends $e_1$ to $u$. Choose $0<\theta<\pi/2$ with $\cos\theta/\sqrt d-\sin\theta>0$, and set $r_0=1/2$. For any cone vector $z$, $z_1>|z|\cos\theta$ and $|z-z_1e_1|<|z|\sin\theta$. Hence $\sigma_j(Q_xz)_j\ge z_1/\sqrt d-|z-z_1e_1|>|z|(\cos\theta/\sqrt d-\sin\theta)>0$ for each coordinate. Each coordinate moves toward the cube's interior by less than $r_0$, so $x+Q_xz\in(0,1)^d$.

Distinct midpoint sites have fill distance at most $\sqrt d/(2m)$. Since $m$ is odd, $x_0\in X_m$. By continuity in [F2], choose $0<\delta_m<1/(4m)$ so that $|1-k(\delta_me_1)|<1/m$. Strict positive definiteness for the two distinct sites $x_0$ and $x_0+\delta_me_1$ makes $1-k(\delta_me_1)>0$, so in fact $0<1-k(\delta_me_1)<1/m$. Let $Z_m=X_m\cup\{x_0+\delta_me_1\}$. The new site is in the cube and is distinct from all grid sites, its separation radius satisfies $q_{Z_m}\le\delta_m/2<1$, and adding a site cannot increase fill distance. Thus $h_{Z_m}\le\sqrt d/(2m)\to0$.

Let $u$ be the unit vector with entries $1/\sqrt2$ and $-1/\sqrt2$ at the new site and $x_0$, and zero elsewhere. The corresponding Rayleigh quotient is $$u^{\mathsf T}K_{Z_m}u=\tfrac12(1+1-2k(\delta_me_1))=1-k(\delta_me_1).$$ Hence [F3] gives $0<\lambda_{\min}(K_{Z_m})\le1-k(\delta_me_1)<1/m$. Every diagonal entry is $1$, so $\operatorname{tr}K_{Z_m}=|Z_m|$; positivity of the eigenvalues implies $\lambda_{\max}(K_{Z_m})\ge1$. Consequently $\kappa_2(K_{Z_m})\ge1/\lambda_{\min}(K_{Z_m})>m$. Together with step 1.2, this gives fill distance tending to zero and condition number tending to infinity.
